title: Generalist raises another $200M for robot brains, hits $3B valuation
subtitle: The DeepMind- and Boston Dynamics-spinoff has pulled in $600M in two months as investors bet on general-purpose control models for physical robots.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Robotics startup Generalist has quietly closed another $200 million in funding, roughly two months after a $400 million round, according to reports first published on August 24 by Axios and confirmed the next day by TechCrunch. 8VC led the extension, joined by Nvidia, Bezos Expeditions, Radical Ventures, USV, Spark Capital, and Fei-Fei Li. The company's valuation has moved above $3 billion, up from $2 billion in June. The combined $600 million raised this summer makes Generalist one of the best-funded startups in embodied AI.

Generalist was founded in 2024 by two former Google DeepMind researchers, Pete Florence and Andy Zeng, and former Boston Dynamics engineer Andrew Barry. Their thesis is that the bottleneck in useful robots is not the hardware — plenty of factories can build a decent arm — but the general-purpose control model that lets a robot pick up an unfamiliar object, open a drawer it hasn't seen, or recover from a bump. The company is building that model directly, in the same way OpenAI built GPT for language, and licensing it to hardware partners rather than shipping its own robot.

The pace of capital flowing into robot foundation models is now comparable to the LLM boom of 2023. Physical Intelligence, Skild, Figure, 1X, and Generalist have collectively raised well over $5 billion in the last twelve months, and Nvidia now appears on almost every cap table — a signal that the incumbent GPU vendor is hedging across the entire field rather than picking a winner. What is still unclear is which of these companies will get to a demonstrated general-purpose policy first, and whether that policy will need to be trained per-embodiment or will transfer across arms.

For learners: the interesting question in embodied AI right now is the same one that dominated LLMs in 2022 — how much of intelligence is a scaling problem and how much requires a genuinely new idea. The people betting on scaling say a bigger model trained on more robot-video data will keep unlocking new behaviors, the way GPT-3 unlocked few-shot prompting. If you want to follow this field, watch the benchmark scores on tasks the models weren't trained on. That's where the argument will be settled.
